message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is a concise overview of the most important rights you have as a tenant in Texas: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it cannot exceed **one month’s rent** for an unfurnished unit or **two months’ rent** for a furnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after the lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written record of the deposit amount and any receipts.
• Request a written itemized list of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must maintain the premises in a **safe and livable condition** (e.g., proper heating, plumbing, electrical, structural integrity).
• The landlord must keep the property in good repair and comply with all building, housing, and health codes. | • Document any maintenance issues with photos and written notices.
• If the landlord fails to address serious problems, you may have the right to withhold rent or repair and deduct. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Texas law does not require a specific notice period for late rent, but many leases include a **late fee** clause. | • Review your lease for any late fee provisions.
• If the lease is silent, the landlord cannot charge a late fee. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For a **month‑to‑month** tenancy, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** to terminate.
• For a **fixed‑term** lease, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** if they intend to terminate before the lease expires. | • Provide written notice if you plan to move out early.
• Keep copies of all notices sent and received. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering the premises, except in emergencies. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you may have a right to sue for trespass. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Texas Fair Housing Act**, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report any discriminatory practices to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair the issue yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure (e.g., give written notice, keep receipts). | • Keep receipts and a written record of the repair. | | **Lease Modification** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | • Do not sign a new lease or amendment unless you agree to the terms. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction procedures, which include providing a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment of rent).
• The landlord must file a lawsuit in court to obtain a writ of possession. | • If you receive an eviction notice, respond promptly and consider seeking legal advice. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Tenants can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek a **writ of possession** if the landlord unlawfully holds onto the property. | • Keep all documentation (lease, receipts, correspondence) to support any legal action. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, especially regarding rent, maintenance, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, text messages, and photos of any maintenance issues. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, send notices and requests via email or certified mail so you have a record. 4. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code (Chapter 92) and the Texas Fair Housing Act. 5. **Seek Legal Help** – If you face a dispute, consult a tenant‑rights organization or a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. ### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on tenant rights, how to file complaints, and consumer protection laws. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Handles discrimination complaints and provides guidance on fair housing. | | **Texas Legal Services Center** | Free legal assistance for low‑income residents, including landlord‑tenant disputes. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Groups** | Many cities have nonprofit organizations that offer workshops, legal clinics, and mediation services. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, a reasonable notice period for termination, protection against discrimination, and the ability to withhold rent or repair and deduct if the landlord fails to maintain the property. Always keep written records and seek professional help if you encounter a dispute.
